section.title: Theme D: Religion, peace and conflict
section.blurb: Violence, terrorism, reasons for war, just war, holy war, pacifism, nuclear weapons, peacemaking and how religious people respond to victims of war.

topics.title: Peace, justice, forgiveness and reconciliation
topics.overview: AQA asks for the meaning and significance of four key ideas: peace, justice, forgiveness and reconciliation. Learn a clear definition of each, why it matters to Christians, Jews and non-religious people, and a source you can quote for each.

bullets: **Conflict** is a serious disagreement or argument between individuals, groups or nations. It can grow into **war**, which is armed fighting between nations or between groups within a nation.
Religion matters here because Christians and Jews believe humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), so every life is sacred. This is the **sanctity of life**.
Religion has both encouraged peace and been used to justify war. The rest of this theme looks at both sides.
**Peace** is the absence of conflict, but it is more than that: it means harmony, safety and people living well together.

Significance for Christians: Jesus is called the 'Prince of Peace' (Isaiah 9:6). He said 'Peace I leave with you' (John 14:27) and 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9). Christians speak of peace with God (through Jesus) and peace with other people. Many churches share 'the peace' (a handshake or greeting) in services.

Significance for Jews: the Hebrew word **shalom** means peace, wholeness and well-being, and is used as a greeting. Hillel taught Jews to be 'loving peace and pursuing peace' (Pirkei Avot 1:12). The prophets look forward to a messianic age when 'nation will not take up sword against nation' (Isaiah 2:4, Micah 4:3).
Non-religious significance: humanists value peace because war destroys the one life people have and their happiness. The United Nations was founded in 1945 to keep international peace.
**Justice** means bringing about what is right and fair, according to the law, or making up for a wrong that has been done.

Significance: many believers say real peace is impossible without justice, because unfairness (poverty, oppression, discrimination) makes people angry and leads to conflict. Pope Paul VI said in 1972: 'If you want peace, work for justice.'

Christian teaching: the prophets demand justice: 'Let justice roll on like rivers' (Amos 5:24) and 'act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God' (Micah 6:8). Jesus overturned the money changers' tables in the Temple because of unfairness (John 2:15).

Jewish teaching: 'Justice, justice you shall pursue' (Deuteronomy 16:20). The Mishnah says the world stands on three things: justice, truth and peace (Pirkei Avot 1:18). **Tzedek** (justice) is linked to **tzedakah** (charity), which is seen as a duty, not a choice.

Non-religious: humanists and many atheists support human rights, fair laws and international courts as the way to achieve justice. A war might be fought to restore justice, for example to stop genocide, which is why justice links to just war theory.
**Forgiveness** means showing grace and mercy and pardoning someone for what they have done wrong, letting go of anger and the wish for revenge.

Christian teaching: in the Lord's Prayer Christians ask God to 'forgive us our sins as we forgive those who sin against us'. Jesus told Peter to forgive 'seventy times seven' times (Matthew 18:22) and forgave the soldiers who crucified him (Luke 23:34). Forgiveness does not mean pretending a wrong did not happen, and it can sit alongside justice.

Jewish teaching: on **Yom Kippur** (Day of Atonement) God forgives sins against God, but for wrongs done to another person you must first put things right and ask that person for forgiveness (Mishnah Yoma 8:9). This links forgiveness to **teshuvah** (repentance). Some Jews teach that only the victim can forgive, so murder or genocide cannot be forgiven by others on the victim's behalf.
Significance after war: forgiveness can stop cycles of revenge. Some victims and nations find it impossible, and say forgiveness must not mean letting war criminals escape justice.

Non-religious: many humanists see forgiveness as good for the victim's own well-being and for society. **The Forgiveness Project**, a secular UK charity founded in 2004, shares real stories of victims and offenders to show that forgiveness is possible, without saying anyone must forgive.
**Reconciliation** means restoring friendly relationships after conflict or disagreement: former enemies learn to live and work together again.

Christian teaching: Christians believe Jesus reconciled people with God, and God 'gave to us the ministry of reconciliation' (2 Corinthians 5:18). Jesus said to make peace with your brother before offering a gift at the altar (Matthew 5:23-24). Catholics call confession the **sacrament of reconciliation**.

Example: Coventry Cathedral was destroyed by bombing in November 1940. The words 'Father forgive' were later inscribed on the ruined wall, and its **Community of the Cross of Nails** still works for reconciliation in places of conflict today, starting with links to Germany.

Example: after apartheid in South Africa, Archbishop Desmond Tutu chaired the **Truth and Reconciliation Commission** (from 1996), where victims could tell their stories and offenders who told the full truth could apply for amnesty.

Jewish teaching: Aaron is remembered as a peacemaker who reconciled people (Pirkei Avot 1:12). Making peace between people (shalom bayit in the home, and between neighbours) is a mitzvah. Yom Kippur is a yearly time for reconciliation with God and others.

Non-religious: reconciliation is seen as practical: without it, old conflicts restart. Peace processes such as the Good Friday Agreement (1998) in Northern Ireland include work to rebuild trust between communities.

views.label: Christian
views.text: Peace, justice, forgiveness and reconciliation are all part of God's plan. Jesus said peacemakers will be called children of God, taught people to forgive again and again, and gave his followers a 'ministry of reconciliation'.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Shalom is a gift from God and a duty for people, and the world stands on justice, truth and peace. Forgiveness for harming another person requires repentance and asking that person directly, especially before Yom Kippur.

views.label: Non-religious
views.text: Peace and justice matter because humans have only one life and deserve to flourish. These values come from reason and empathy rather than God, and are best protected by human rights, international law and talking through disputes.

topics.title: Violence, violent protest and terrorism
topics.overview: Violence is one of AQA's three 'contrasting beliefs' issues for Theme D, so you must explain different views on it from Christianity and at least one other religion. You also need views on protest, violent protest and terrorism, with up-to-date UK examples.

bullets: **Violence** is using actions that threaten or harm others, physically or emotionally. It ranges from a fight in the street to riots, terrorism and war.
Most religious people see violence as wrong because it harms people made in God's image and breaks the commandment 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13).
But views differ on whether violence is ever justified: for example in **self-defence**, to protect someone weaker, or to stop a greater evil. This is where the contrasting beliefs come in.

**Pacifist Christians** (for example Quakers and Mennonites) say violence is never right. Jesus told Peter, 'Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword' (Matthew 26:52), and taught 'turn to him the other also' (Matthew 5:39) and 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44).

**Most Christians** (including Catholic and Anglican teaching) say violence should be avoided but force can be a last resort to defend yourself or protect others. The Catholic Catechism allows legitimate self-defence, and just war theory applies the same idea to nations.

Some Christians point out that Jesus used force against injustice when he made a whip and overturned the money changers' tables (John 2:15), and told the disciples to buy a sword (Luke 22:36). Others reply that these were not attacks on people.
Christians are also taught to leave revenge to God: 'Don't seek revenge yourselves... overcome evil with good' (Romans 12:19-21).
Judaism values peace and life very highly. Saving a life (**pikuach nefesh**) overrides almost every other commandment, and 'You shall not endanger the life of your neighbour' (Leviticus 19:16).

But Judaism is **not pacifist**. The Torah allows a person to defend themselves: if a burglar breaking in at night is killed, there is no bloodguilt (Exodus 22:2). The Talmud teaches, 'If someone comes to kill you, rise and kill him first' (Sanhedrin 72a).
Violence must be the minimum needed to protect life, never revenge: 'You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge' (Leviticus 19:18).
So a contrast you can use: Quakers say violence is never right; Judaism says violence is wrong except to defend life.

A **protest** is an expression of disapproval, often in a public group. In the UK peaceful protest is a legal right (Human Rights Act 1998, Articles 10 and 11), but the police can put conditions on protests, and the Public Order Act 2023 created new offences, for example for 'locking on' to block roads.
**Violent protest** includes rioting, attacking people or seriously damaging property. It is illegal in the UK.

Christian examples of non-violent protest: Martin Luther King, a Baptist minister, led marches and boycotts against racism in the USA in the 1950s and 1960s. Today Christian Climate Action and many church groups hold vigils and marches.

Some argue violent protest can be justified if peaceful protest is ignored, pointing to some Suffragettes who smashed windows. Others reply that violence harms innocent people, loses public support and makes change harder.

Non-religious views: humanists support freedom of speech and the right to protest peacefully, but reject violence that harms others. A **utilitarian** would ask whether a protest's consequences bring the greatest good for the greatest number; violence usually causes more harm than good.

**Terrorism** is the unlawful use of violence, usually against the public, to further a political or religious cause. UK law (Terrorism Act 2000) includes serious violence, threats and serious damage to property done to influence the government or intimidate the public.

Examples in the UK: the London bombings of 7 July 2005 (52 people killed), the Manchester Arena attack in 2017 (22 killed) and the attack on Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue in Manchester on Yom Kippur, 2 October 2025, in which two people were killed.

As of November 2026 the UK national threat level is **severe** (an attack is highly likely). It was raised from substantial on 30 April 2026, after a stabbing attack on the Jewish community in Golders Green, London.

In July 2025 the UK government banned (proscribed) the direct action group Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation after damage to RAF aircraft. Supporters and human rights groups argued this treated protest as terrorism; the government argued serious property damage meets the legal definition. The Court of Appeal ruled the ban lawful in June 2026. This shows how people disagree about where protest ends and terrorism begins.

Religious responses: Christian and Jewish leaders condemn terrorism, even when the attacker claims a religious cause, because it deliberately kills innocent people, ignores the sanctity of life and cannot bring true peace. They often respond with prayer vigils, interfaith solidarity and support for victims.
Non-religious response: terrorism is wrong because it violates human rights and the right to life, and uses fear rather than argument.

views.label: Pacifist Christian
views.text: Violence is never right, even in self-defence. Jesus told Peter to put away his sword and taught his followers to turn the other cheek and love their enemies, so conflict should be met with non-violent action.

views.label: Most Christians
views.text: Violence should be avoided and peaceful protest is the right way to challenge injustice, but limited force can be a last resort to defend yourself or protect the innocent. Terrorism and violent protest that harm innocent people are condemned.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Peace and life are precious, so violence for revenge is forbidden. But the Torah and Talmud allow force in self-defence, 'if someone comes to kill you, rise and kill him first', and saving life (pikuach nefesh) can require it.

views.label: Humanist
views.text: The right to protest peacefully is a key freedom, but violence that harms people is wrong because everyone has only one life. Disputes should be solved by reason, evidence and democratic means.

views.label: Utilitarian
views.text: Judges violence by its results: is it the action that brings the greatest good for the greatest number? Usually violent protest and terrorism cause far more suffering than good, though force to stop a greater harm might be justified.

pitfalls: Examiners noted many answers on violence only said 'violence is wrong'. Show the contrast: never right (pacifists) versus allowed in self-defence (most Christians, Judaism).
Do not say any religion 'supports terrorism'. Mainstream Christian and Jewish teaching condemns attacks on innocent people, even when attackers claim a religious motive.
Do not confuse protest with violent protest. Peaceful protest is widely supported by religious people; the debate is about violence.

topics.title: Reasons for war: greed, self-defence and retaliation
topics.overview: AQA names greed, self-defence and retaliation as reasons for war. Know what each means, a real example, and how Christians, Jews and non-religious people judge each one.

bullets: **Greed**: selfish desire for more, for example land, oil, minerals or power. Example: Iraq's invasion of oil-rich Kuwait in 1990.

**Self-defence**: acting to protect yourself, your country or allies from attack. Example: Ukraine has fought in self-defence since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Article 51 of the UN Charter recognises a nation's right to self-defence.

**Retaliation**: deliberately harming someone in return for harm they have done, hitting back. Retaliation can look like self-defence, but its aim is to punish or get even, not to stop an attack that is happening.
Other causes you can mention: ideology or religion, defending an ally, protecting people from genocide (humanitarian intervention), and civil war (fighting between groups inside one country).

**Greed** is condemned. The Ten Commandments forbid coveting (Exodus 20:17), 'the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' (1 Timothy 6:10), and James asks where wars come from and answers that they come from selfish desires (James 4:1-2).
**Self-defence** is accepted by most Christians as a just cause under just war theory, as long as the other criteria are met. Pacifist Christians reject even defensive war.

**Retaliation** is rejected because Jesus replaced 'an eye for an eye' with 'turn to him the other also' (Matthew 5:38-39), and Paul taught 'Repay no one evil for evil' and to leave vengeance to God (Romans 12:17-19).
Some Christians accept that defending others can involve striking back to stop further attacks, but they distinguish this from revenge.

**Self-defence** is a duty. A war of defence is an obligatory war (**milchemet mitzvah**), in which everyone must take part (Mishnah Sotah 8:7). The Talmud allows striking first against someone about to attack (Sanhedrin 72a), so some Jews accept a pre-emptive strike when an attack is certain.

**Greed**: an optional war (**milchemet reshut**), for example to expand territory, needed the approval of the Great Sanhedrin of 71 judges (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:5). With no Sanhedrin today, most Jews say only defensive wars are acceptable.

**Retaliation**: 'You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge' (Leviticus 19:18). 'An eye for an eye' (Exodus 21:24) was understood by the rabbis as fair compensation in court, not permission for revenge.
Many Jews link the right of self-defence to Jewish history, including the Holocaust: a people must be able to protect itself.
International law accepts self-defence (UN Charter Article 51) but forbids aggression and wars of revenge or conquest.
Humanists judge war by its consequences and by human rights: wars of greed and revenge cause huge suffering for no good reason, while defending people from attack may be justified.
A utilitarian would ask whether war produces the greatest good for the greatest number. Retaliation often starts a cycle of violence that causes more harm overall.

Britain entered the Second World War in September 1939 because Germany invaded Poland, which Britain had promised to defend. It was not because of the Holocaust, which most of the world did not fully know about until later.
Self-defence must be a response to a real attack or a clear and immediate threat. Hitting back weeks later to punish is retaliation.

views.label: Just war Christian
views.text: Self-defence, including defending other nations, can be a just cause if war is a last resort. Greed and revenge are wrong because Jesus taught love of neighbour and not repaying evil for evil.

views.label: Pacifist Christian
views.text: No reason, not even self-defence, makes war right. Jesus told his followers to turn the other cheek, and every war kills people made in God's image.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Defending the community is an obligatory war and a duty, because saving life is vital. Wars of greed need authority that no longer exists, and revenge is forbidden by the Torah.

views.label: Non-religious
views.text: Self-defence is a legitimate reason for war under international law, but greed and retaliation cause needless suffering and cannot be justified by their consequences.

topics.title: Nuclear weapons, deterrence and weapons of mass destruction
topics.overview: Weapons of mass destruction (WMD) is one of AQA's three 'contrasting beliefs' issues. Know the difference between using WMD and having them as a deterrent, the arguments on each side, and up-to-date facts about the UK and nuclear treaties (as of November 2026).

bullets: **Weapons of mass destruction (WMD)** are weapons that can kill large numbers of people and cause great damage, without distinguishing soldiers from civilians. There are three main kinds: **nuclear**, **chemical** (poison gases such as sarin or nerve agents) and **biological** (germs or viruses used as weapons).

Nuclear bombs have been used in war only twice, on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in Japan in August 1945. Around 140,000 people had died in Hiroshima by the end of 1945, and many survivors suffered cancers and other illnesses for decades.

Chemical weapons are banned by the Chemical Weapons Convention (in force 1997) and biological weapons by the Biological Weapons Convention (1972), but chemical weapons have still been used, for example in Syria's civil war.

notes.h: Nuclear deterrence and the UK (facts as of November 2026)
bullets: **Nuclear deterrence** is the idea that having nuclear weapons stops other countries from attacking, because they fear devastating retaliation.

The UK has had a submarine always at sea with Trident nuclear missiles since 1969. New Dreadnought-class submarines are being built to replace the Vanguard class in the 2030s. In 2021 the UK raised the cap on its warhead stockpile to 260, and in June 2025 it announced it would buy F-35A jets able to carry NATO nuclear weapons.

Treaties: under the **Non-Proliferation Treaty** (NPT, 1970) the UK is one of five recognised nuclear-weapon states and has promised to work towards disarmament. The 2026 NPT Review Conference (April to May 2026) ended without agreement. The last US-Russia arms control treaty, **New START**, expired on 5 February 2026.

The **Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons** (TPNW) bans nuclear weapons completely and came into force in January 2021. By late 2025 more than 70 countries had ratified it, but none of the nine nuclear-armed states, including the UK, has joined.
Deterrence: no two nuclear-armed powers have fought a full-scale war with each other since 1945, which supporters say shows deterrence works.
They protect a country and its allies from attack or blackmail by other nuclear states.
Some Christians and Jews accept possession as the **lesser evil**, while saying actual use could never be justified.

notes.h: Arguments against having or using them
bullets: Use would kill huge numbers of civilians, breaking the just war rules of **proportionality** and **discrimination** (not targeting civilians) and the commandment 'You shall not murder'.
They destroy God's creation: radiation and nuclear winter could damage the earth for generations. The Torah forbids even cutting down fruit trees in a siege (Deuteronomy 20:19).
Deterrence only works if leaders are willing to use them, which many believers say is itself immoral.
Risks of accidents, hacking, mistakes or terrorists getting them. The money (billions of pounds) could be spent on health, education or helping the poor.

**Catholic**: Pope Francis said in 2017 that the threat of using nuclear weapons, and even possessing them, is to be firmly condemned, and in Hiroshima in 2019 called possession immoral. In May 2026 Pope Leo XIV said 'the Church has spoken out against all nuclear weapons'. Pax Christi campaigns for disarmament.

**Church of England**: in 1983 the General Synod rejected the UK giving up its nuclear weapons alone (unilateral disarmament) but said first use could never be morally justified. In 2018 Synod voted (260 to 26) to urge the government to respond positively to the TPNW. It has not called on the UK to scrap Trident immediately.
**Quakers and Methodists** oppose nuclear weapons and campaign for disarmament; Christian CND is a Christian campaign group.

**Judaism**: life is sacred and the whole world is destroyed when one life is destroyed (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5), so WMD use is seen as wrong. A Talmud passage (Shevuot 35b) is often explained as forbidding a war that would kill more than a sixth of the population, which WMD would break. Some Jews argue that after the Holocaust a small nation needs a deterrent; Israel is widely believed to have nuclear weapons but has never confirmed it.

**Non-religious**: some support deterrence for security. CND (founded 1958) and many humanists oppose nuclear weapons. A utilitarian could argue either way: deterrence may prevent war, but one use could cause unimaginable suffering.

views.label: Catholic
views.text: Teaches that using nuclear weapons, threatening to use them and even possessing them is immoral. Popes since 2017 have called for complete disarmament, and Pope Leo XIV said in 2026 that the Church opposes all nuclear weapons.

views.label: Quaker
views.text: Opposes all nuclear weapons absolutely, as part of a Peace Testimony that rejects all war. Campaigns for disarmament and believes there is that of God in everyone who would be killed.

views.label: Church of England
views.text: Has accepted deterrence as a lesser evil in a dangerous world, while saying that first use could never be justified, and now urges the government to work towards a world without nuclear weapons.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Mass killing of innocent people can never be justified because each life is like a whole world, but some believe a nation surrounded by enemies may need a deterrent after the Holocaust.

views.label: Non-religious
views.text: Divided: some support deterrence for national security, while others, such as campaigners for disarmament, argue the cost, the risk and the scale of possible suffering outweigh any benefit.

topics.tip: Read the question carefully: is it about using WMD or having them (deterrence)? Religions are united against use; they disagree about possession. That difference gives you an easy 'different beliefs' answer.
pitfalls: Examiners in 2024 and 2025 saw many answers about using WMD when the question was about having them. Answers that only discussed use gained no marks.
WMD are not only nuclear. Chemical and biological weapons are easy to argue against and are already banned by treaties, so mention them.
Do not claim any religion supports actually using WMD. Some believers accept possession as a deterrent, which is different.

topics.title: The just war theory
topics.overview: Just war theory is the main Christian way of deciding whether a war can be right and how it must be fought. Learn the criteria, who developed them, how Jews and non-religious people use similar ideas, and how to evaluate the theory today.

bullets: The **just war theory** is a set of criteria for judging whether it is right to go to war and how a war should be fought.
St Augustine of Hippo (354 to 430 CE) argued that Christians could fight to restore peace and justice, but only with the right attitude and never out of love of violence.
St Thomas Aquinas (13th century) set out three conditions in his Summa Theologiae: proper authority, a just cause and right intention. Later thinkers added the other criteria.
The Catholic Catechism (paragraph 2309) still lists strict conditions for 'legitimate defence by military force', and many other Christians accept the theory as a realistic guide.
**Just cause**: for example self-defence, defending others or stopping genocide. Not greed or revenge.
**Legitimate authority**: the war must be declared by a proper government (today often linked to the UN), not by individuals or private groups.
**Right intention**: the aim must be to restore peace and justice, not to gain land or take revenge.
**Last resort**: all peaceful methods (talks, sanctions, the UN) must have been tried first.
**Reasonable chance of success**: lives should not be wasted on a war that cannot be won.
**Proportionality**: the good achieved must outweigh the harm caused, and no more force should be used than needed.
**Discrimination**: civilians must not be deliberately targeted; only soldiers are legitimate targets.
Some lists split these into rules for going to war (**jus ad bellum**) and rules for fighting it (**jus in bello**).

Christians have used the theory to judge real wars. Many saw the Second World War against Nazi Germany as just. In 2003 Pope John Paul II and Archbishop Rowan Williams both raised serious doubts about the invasion of Iraq, partly because it lacked clear UN approval and peaceful options had not run out.
Strengths: it limits war, protects civilians, makes leaders justify their actions, and does not leave the innocent undefended.

Weaknesses: people disagree about whether each rule is met; both sides usually claim their cause is just; modern weapons (bombing cities, drones, WMD) make proportionality and discrimination very hard; pacifists say no war fits Jesus' teaching.
Pope Leo XIV said in May 2026 that the nuclear age has made just war discussion 'a very complex problem' and that dialogue is better than seeking weapons.

Judaism distinguishes an obligatory war (**milchemet mitzvah**), such as self-defence, from an optional war (**milchemet reshut**), which needed the approval of the Sanhedrin of 71 judges (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:5).

The Torah limits warfare: peace must be offered first (Deuteronomy 20:10), fruit trees must not be destroyed (Deuteronomy 20:19), and Jewish tradition (Maimonides) says a besieged city should be surrounded on three sides only, so those who want to flee can escape.
These rules are similar to last resort, proportionality and discrimination.

International law contains many just war ideas: the UN Charter allows self-defence (Article 51) and force approved by the UN Security Council, and the Geneva Conventions protect civilians and prisoners.
Many non-religious people accept just war thinking on human rights grounds. A utilitarian supports a war only if it will bring about less suffering overall than not fighting.

views.label: Catholic

views.label: Jewish

views.label: Non-religious
views.text: International law uses similar ideas, such as self-defence, proportionality and protecting civilians, based on human rights rather than God.

Examiners credit knowledge of the criteria only when it is applied to the question. Choose the criteria most relevant (for example discrimination for a question about civilians).

topics.title: Holy war and religion as a cause of war and violence
topics.overview: AQA asks about holy war and about religion and belief as a cause of war and violence in the contemporary world. Know what makes a war 'holy', historical and modern examples, and the arguments for and against the claim that religion causes war.

bullets: A **holy war** is fighting for a religious cause or God, probably controlled by a religious leader. Fighters believe God is on their side and may expect spiritual rewards.
A war is not holy just because soldiers are religious. Religion must be the reason for fighting, for example to defend the faith, win back holy places or spread the religion.
Holy war is different from just war: just war is about fair reasons and limits that anyone can judge; holy war rests on a belief that God commands it.
In the Hebrew Bible, God is called 'a man of war' (Exodus 15:3) and promises to fight for Israel (Deuteronomy 20:4); the conquest of Canaan under Joshua is described as commanded by God.

The **Maccabees** fought the Greek ruler Antiochus IV in the 2nd century BCE after he banned Jewish practice and defiled the Temple. Jews remember their victory and the rededication of the Temple at Hanukkah. Many see this as a fight for religious freedom.

The **Crusades** were a series of wars from 1095 onwards, called by popes (starting with Pope Urban II), to win control of Jerusalem and the Holy Land. Crusaders were promised forgiveness of sins. They involved terrible massacres, including of Jews in Europe and of Muslims and Jews in Jerusalem in 1099.
In 2000 Pope John Paul II led a 'Day of Pardon' asking forgiveness for sins committed by Christians in the past, including violence in the service of the faith.

Most Christians today reject holy war. Jesus taught love of enemies (Matthew 5:44), his kingdom is 'not of this world' (John 18:36), and faith cannot be forced on anyone. Some Christians accept that defending religious freedom could be a just cause, but under just war rules, not as a holy war.

Most Jews today do not believe in holy war. Wars commanded by God in the Bible are seen as belonging to a particular time; with no prophet, Temple or Sanhedrin, there is no authority to declare one. Defensive war is still accepted.

A modern example that shocked many Christians: in March 2024 the World Russian People's Council, headed by Patriarch Kirill of the Russian Orthodox Church, called Russia's war in Ukraine a 'Holy War'. The World Council of Churches and many church leaders rejected the idea that the invasion could be holy.

notes.h: Religion and belief as a cause of war and violence today
bullets: Arguments that religion causes conflict: religious differences can create 'us and them' identities; disputes over holy places (for example Jerusalem); extremists use religious language to justify terrorism; leaders may say God supports their side.

Examples often given: the Troubles in Northern Ireland (1968 to 1998), where Catholic and Protestant identities were linked to nationalist and unionist politics; the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, with disputes over land and holy sites; terrorist groups that claim a religious cause.

Arguments against: most conflicts are mainly about land, power, money, history and national identity, and religion is used as a label or excuse. In Northern Ireland the core dispute was whether it should belong to the UK or Ireland.
Non-religious **beliefs** can also cause war: political ideologies such as fascism and communism led to the Second World War and many 20th century conflicts.
Religion also drives peacemaking: Corrymeela, Pax Christi, the Community of Sant'Egidio and many interfaith groups work to end conflicts.
Some atheists, such as Richard Dawkins, argue that faith (belief without evidence) makes people certain they are right and so can make violence easier to justify.

Others, including many humanists and historians, argue that religion is rarely the only cause, and that secular ideologies have caused enormous wars too. Humanists support freedom of belief for everyone as a way to reduce conflict.

views.label: Most Christians today

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Wars commanded by God in scripture belonged to a particular time, and there is no authority to declare one today. Defensive wars are accepted, but the focus is on pursuing peace.

views.label: Russian Orthodox leadership

views.label: Atheist critic

views.label: Humanist
views.text: Religion is rarely the only cause of war; land, power and political ideologies matter more. Protecting freedom of belief for all is the best way to stop religion being used to fuel conflict.

topics.title: Pacifism and religious peacemaking today
topics.overview: Pacifism is one of AQA's three 'contrasting beliefs' issues, so you need contrasting Christian and Jewish views. AQA also asks about religion and peacemaking in the contemporary world, including the work of named individuals influenced by religious teaching.

bullets: **Pacifism** is the belief that people should not take part in war or any serious violence, especially for religious or moral reasons.

**Absolute pacifists** say violence is always wrong, even in self-defence. **Relative (or conditional) pacifists** reject war in general but accept that force might be needed in extreme cases, or reject modern warfare because of WMD.
Pacifists are not passive. Many work actively for peace and justice through protest, aid and reconciliation, and some serve in non-combat roles, such as medics or ambulance drivers.

A **conscientious objector** refuses to fight on grounds of conscience. In the First World War, around 16,000 British men registered as conscientious objectors; some were imprisoned. Desmond Doss, a Seventh-day Adventist, served as an unarmed medic in the Second World War and saved around 75 men at Okinawa.

**Quakers** (the Religious Society of Friends) hold a **Peace Testimony**. In 1660 they declared to King Charles II that they 'utterly deny all outward wars and strife'. They believe there is 'that of God in everyone', so killing anyone is wrong. Mennonites, the Anglican Pacifist Fellowship and the Fellowship of Reconciliation also hold pacifist views.

Pacifist sources: 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9), turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:39), love your enemies (Matthew 5:44), Jesus telling Peter to put away his sword (Matthew 26:52), and the fact that many early Christians refused to serve in the Roman army.

**Most Christians** (including Catholic and Anglican teaching) are not absolute pacifists. They value peace highly but accept that force may sometimes be needed to protect the innocent, using just war theory. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a German Lutheran pastor and former pacifist, joined resistance to Hitler and was executed in 1945.
Arguments against pacifism: it may leave innocent people undefended; some evils (such as genocide) may only be stopped by force; it relies on others to defend the pacifist's freedom.
Judaism values peace very highly: 'seek peace and pursue it' (Psalm 34:14), and Hillel taught to be 'loving peace and pursuing peace' (Pirkei Avot 1:12).
But mainstream Judaism is **not pacifist**. Self-defence and defensive war (milchemet mitzvah) are allowed and can be a duty, because saving life (pikuach nefesh) is so important.

A minority of Jews are pacifists. The Jewish Peace Fellowship (founded in the USA in 1941) supports Jewish conscientious objectors, and some draw on the prophets' vision of a world without war (Micah 4:3).
So the contrast is clear: Quakers say war is always wrong; most Jews say war is sometimes necessary to protect life.

Some non-religious people are pacifists on moral grounds. The Peace Pledge Union (founded 1934) is a British pacifist group open to people of any belief or none. The philosopher Bertrand Russell, an atheist, was imprisoned in 1918 for his anti-war campaigning.
Others, including many humanists, accept that force can be justified to protect people's lives and rights. A utilitarian rejects absolute rules and asks which choice will cause least suffering.

notes.h: Religious peacemaking in the contemporary world
bullets: **Peacemaking** is the action of trying to establish peace: preventing conflict, ending it and rebuilding relationships afterwards.

**Corrymeela** (founded 1965 by Ray Davey, a Presbyterian chaplain) is a Christian community in Ballycastle, Northern Ireland, that brings Catholics, Protestants and others together. It marked 60 years of peacebuilding in 2025.

**Pax Christi** is an international Catholic peace movement working for peace, disarmament and non-violence. The **Community of Sant'Egidio**, a Catholic lay movement, helped negotiate the 1992 peace agreement that ended Mozambique's civil war and still mediates in conflicts today.
**Leymah Gbowee**, a Liberian Christian, organised Christian and Muslim women to pray and protest for peace, helping end Liberia's civil war in 2003. She shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2011.

**Pope Leo XIV**, elected in May 2025, began his papacy calling for a peace that is 'unarmed and disarming'. In April 2026 the new Archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, publicly backed his calls for peace in the Middle East.

Jewish peacemaking: **Rabbis for Human Rights** (founded in Israel in 1988) works for justice and human rights for Israelis and Palestinians; the **Council of Christians and Jews** (founded in the UK in 1942) builds understanding between faiths. Many synagogues join interfaith projects.

Historic individuals still often used: Martin Luther King (non-violent civil rights campaigner, Baptist minister) and Archbishop Desmond Tutu (Truth and Reconciliation Commission in South Africa, died 2021).

Ways individual believers act as peacemakers: praying for peace, mediating in disputes, forgiving, joining peace groups, campaigning against war, interfaith dialogue, working as a medic rather than fighting.

views.label: Catholic
views.text: Teaches that peace is the goal and force is a last resort under strict just war conditions. Popes call for disarmament and dialogue, and movements such as Pax Christi and Sant'Egidio work for peace.

views.label: Other Christian
views.text: Many Christians say they should be peacemakers while accepting that force may sometimes be needed to stop greater evil, as Bonhoeffer decided when he resisted Hitler.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Peace is highly valued but the tradition is not pacifist. Defensive force is allowed and can be a duty to save life, yet Jews are taught to love peace and pursue it.

views.label: Non-religious
views.text: Some are pacifists on moral grounds, while others accept fighting if it prevents greater harm and protects human rights.

topics.title: Religious responses to the victims of war
topics.overview: AQA asks why and how religious people help victims of war, including the work of one present-day religious organisation. Learn one organisation in detail (for example Christian Aid or World Jewish Relief) with specific examples, and the teachings that motivate believers.

bullets: Victims of war include people killed or injured, families who lose loved ones or homes, **refugees** forced to flee their country, people displaced inside their own country, children who miss school or are recruited as child soldiers, and soldiers left with physical injuries or trauma.

War also causes hunger, disease and damage to water, power and hospitals that lasts long after the fighting stops. In 2026 some of the world's largest humanitarian crises were caused by war, for example in Sudan, Ukraine and Gaza.
Christians: Jesus commanded 'Love your neighbour as yourself' (Matthew 22:39), and the **parable of the Good Samaritan** (Luke 10:25-37) shows that your neighbour includes strangers and even enemies.

Christians: in the **parable of the Sheep and Goats** Jesus says, 'Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me' (Matthew 25:40), so helping refugees and the wounded is serving Jesus.
Jews: **pikuach nefesh** (saving life) overrides almost every other commandment; **tikkun olam** (repairing the world) and **tzedakah** (charity as a duty of justice) require practical help.

Jews: the Torah says 'love the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt' (Leviticus 19:34, Deuteronomy 10:19). Many Jews also remember that their own families were refugees from persecution.

Both: 'If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat' (Proverbs 25:21) means help should be given to victims on every side. Humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), so every victim has equal dignity.

**Christian Aid** was set up in 1945 by British and Irish churches to help refugees after the Second World War. Today it works with local partners in conflict zones, providing food, clean water, shelter, cash and help rebuilding lives, and it ran a Sudan Crisis Appeal for people fleeing the war there. It also campaigns on the causes of poverty and conflict. Its slogan is 'We believe in life before death'.

**CAFOD** (founded 1962) is the Catholic aid agency for England and Wales and part of **Caritas Internationalis**, a worldwide network of Catholic charities. It provides emergency aid, supports refugees and helps rebuild communities, working through local churches.
**Tearfund** is an evangelical Christian charity that works through local churches in crisis zones.

**World Jewish Relief** began in 1933 (as the Central British Fund) to help Jews escape Nazi Germany, including through the Kindertransport. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 it has provided food, medicine, heating, emergency shelter and repairs to bombed homes for vulnerable people in Ukraine.
**Magen David Adom UK** supports Israel's national emergency medical service, which treats casualties of attacks and war regardless of who they are.

Individual believers help by donating, volunteering, praying, welcoming refugees into their homes (many churches and synagogues supported the UK's Homes for Ukraine scheme in 2022), and campaigning for governments to protect civilians and accept refugees. Military chaplains support soldiers and their families.

Many non-religious people help victims of war out of compassion and a belief in human rights and human dignity. Examples include the British Red Cross and the International Committee of the Red Cross (which, despite its name, is not a religious organisation), Médecins Sans Frontières and Oxfam.
Humanists argue that because this life is the only one we have, relieving suffering now is a moral priority.

views.label: Christian

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Saving life overrides almost every other commandment, and the Torah commands love for the stranger because the people were once strangers in Egypt. Charity is a duty of justice, not an optional extra.

views.label: Non-religious
views.text: Helping victims comes from compassion and respect for human rights. Because this life is the only one, reducing suffering now matters most, through secular charities and international law.
