flashcards.q: What is conflict?
flashcards.a: A serious disagreement between individuals, groups or nations. It can grow into war.

flashcards.q: What is peace, beyond 'no war'?
flashcards.a: Harmony, fairness and safety. In Judaism the word is shalom, which also means wholeness and well-being.

flashcards.q: Define justice.
flashcards.a: Bringing fairness back to a situation, putting wrongs right.

flashcards.q: Define forgiveness.
flashcards.a: Letting go of anger and blame towards someone who has wronged you.

flashcards.q: Define reconciliation.
flashcards.a: Making up and rebuilding a relationship after a conflict.

flashcards.q: Why do Christians and Jews value peace?
flashcards.a: Humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), so life is sacred. Jesus taught love of enemies, and Jewish teaching values shalom.

flashcards.q: Which Bible quote links peacemakers to God?
flashcards.a: 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God' (Matthew 5:9).

flashcards.q: What is the sanctity of life?
flashcards.a: The belief that life is holy because it is created by God.

flashcards.q: Define violence.
flashcards.a: Behaviour using physical force to hurt, kill or damage.

flashcards.q: Define terrorism.
flashcards.a: The use of violence and threats, usually against civilians, to spread fear and force political demands.

flashcards.q: Give two examples of non-violent protest.
flashcards.a: Marches, petitions, vigils, boycotts. Martin Luther King led non-violent protest against racism.

flashcards.q: Why do most Christians reject terrorism?
flashcards.a: It kills innocent people, breaks 'You shall not murder' and goes against Jesus' call to love enemies.

flashcards.q: What Jewish value limits violence?
flashcards.a: Pikuach nefesh, the duty to save life. Force is allowed only to defend life.

flashcards.q: Which verse shows Jesus rejecting violence at his arrest?
flashcards.a: 'Put your sword back in its place, for all who draw the sword will die by the sword' (Matthew 26:52).

flashcards.q: Give a non-religious view on violent protest.
flashcards.a: Some say it can be the lesser evil if peaceful protest is ignored. Many say it harms innocents and makes things worse.

flashcards.q: Name one terrorist attack in the UK that might be used as an example.
flashcards.a: The London bombings of 7 July 2005, or the Manchester Arena attack in 2017.

flashcards.q: Name three reasons for war in the AQA spec.
flashcards.a: Greed, self-defence and retaliation.

flashcards.q: What is greed as a cause of war?
flashcards.a: Fighting to gain land, resources or power. Most religious people see this as wrong.

flashcards.q: Why is self-defence the most accepted reason?
flashcards.a: It protects people from attack. Just war thinking and Jewish teaching on saving life both allow it.

flashcards.q: What is retaliation?
flashcards.a: Hitting back at someone for harming you. It is often condemned because it causes cycles of revenge.

flashcards.q: What is civil war?
flashcards.a: Armed conflict between groups inside one country.

flashcards.q: Which teaching of Jesus argues against retaliation?
flashcards.a: 'Do not repay anyone evil for evil' (Romans 12:17) and turning the other cheek (Matthew 5:39).

flashcards.q: What does international law say about self-defence?
flashcards.a: Article 51 of the UN Charter recognises a state's right to self-defence.

flashcards.q: Give a Jewish view on war for self-defence.
flashcards.a: It is a duty, because saving life (pikuach nefesh) is vital. War of choice needs strong justification.

flashcards.q: What are weapons of mass destruction?
flashcards.a: Weapons causing widespread, indiscriminate damage: nuclear, chemical and biological weapons.

flashcards.q: What is nuclear deterrence?
flashcards.a: Keeping nuclear weapons to put off attackers because of the threat of devastating retaliation.

flashcards.q: When were nuclear weapons used in war?
flashcards.a: August 1945, when the USA bombed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan.

flashcards.q: Give two religious arguments against WMD.
flashcards.a: They kill civilians and break the sanctity of life, and they cannot meet just war rules of proportionality and discrimination.

flashcards.q: Give an argument for keeping nuclear weapons.
flashcards.a: Deterrence: it may prevent attacks and has helped avoid world war since 1945.

flashcards.q: What did Pope Francis say about nuclear weapons in 2017?
flashcards.a: That using nuclear weapons, and even possessing them, should be firmly condemned.

flashcards.q: Which Christian group is strongly opposed to nuclear weapons?
flashcards.a: The Quakers, because of their Peace Testimony.

flashcards.q: Give a non-religious argument against nuclear weapons.
flashcards.a: They cost billions each year, risk accidents and could kill huge numbers of innocents.

flashcards.q: Who first set out Christian ideas on just war, and who developed the criteria?
flashcards.a: St Augustine started the ideas. St Thomas Aquinas developed them in the 13th century.

flashcards.q: List the just war criteria.
flashcards.a: Just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, last resort, reasonable chance of success, proportionality, discrimination.

flashcards.q: What does proportionality mean?
flashcards.a: Using only as much force as needed, with no excessive harm.

flashcards.q: What does legitimate authority mean?
flashcards.a: The war must be declared by a proper government or ruler.

flashcards.q: What does discrimination mean in just war?
flashcards.a: Civilians must not be deliberately attacked.

flashcards.q: What does last resort mean?
flashcards.a: All peaceful ways, such as talks and sanctions, must be tried first.

flashcards.q: What are milchemet mitzvah and milchemet reshut?
flashcards.a: Jewish terms for obligatory war (such as defence) and optional war, which needs stronger authority.

flashcards.q: Give one weakness of the just war theory.
flashcards.a: People disagree about whether the rules are met, and modern weapons make proportionality and discrimination hard.

flashcards.q: What is a holy war?
flashcards.a: A war fought for a religious cause, believed to have God's approval and usually authorised by a religious leader.

flashcards.q: What were the Crusades?
flashcards.a: Christian holy wars from 1095 onwards to take control of the Holy Land, called by the Pope.

flashcards.q: What is the Holy Land?
flashcards.a: Jerusalem and nearby areas, sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims.

flashcards.q: Why do many modern Christians reject holy war?
flashcards.a: It conflicts with Jesus' teaching to love enemies and seek peace.

flashcards.q: Is holy war a main idea in modern Judaism?
flashcards.a: No. Jews accept war mainly for defence, and most focus on peace today.

flashcards.q: Give two examples of conflicts where religion has been a factor.
flashcards.a: The Troubles in Northern Ireland and the Israel-Palestine conflict.

flashcards.q: Why is it hard to say religion is the only cause of a war?
flashcards.a: Most conflicts also involve politics, land, power and identity.

flashcards.q: Give a non-religious view on religion and war.
flashcards.a: Some say religion divides people and causes violence. Others say politics and power are the real causes.

flashcards.q: Define pacifism.
flashcards.a: The belief that war and violence are always wrong.

flashcards.q: What is the Quaker Peace Testimony?
flashcards.a: The Quaker commitment to refuse to fight and to work for peace and justice.

flashcards.q: Who was Desmond Doss?
flashcards.a: A Seventh-day Adventist pacifist who served as an unarmed medic in the Second World War and saved many lives.

flashcards.q: What is Corrymeela?
flashcards.a: A Christian reconciliation community in Northern Ireland founded in 1965 that brings people from different sides together.

flashcards.q: What is Pax Christi?
flashcards.a: A Catholic peace movement that works for peace, justice and disarmament.

flashcards.q: What did Martin Luther King use to campaign against racism?
flashcards.a: Non-violent protest, such as marches and boycotts.

flashcards.q: What did Desmond Tutu do after apartheid?
flashcards.a: Led the South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission to encourage forgiveness and healing.

flashcards.q: Give one argument against pacifism.
flashcards.a: It might leave innocent people undefended against a greater evil.

flashcards.q: Name two Christian organisations that help victims of war.
flashcards.a: Christian Aid and Caritas, including its English and Welsh arm CAFOD.

flashcards.q: When was Christian Aid started and why?
flashcards.a: In 1945, by British and Irish churches, to help refugees.

flashcards.q: Which parables inspire Christians to help victims?
flashcards.a: The Good Samaritan and the Sheep and Goats.

flashcards.q: Give two ways charities help victims of war.
flashcards.a: Emergency food, water and shelter for refugees, and help rebuilding lives and communities.

flashcards.q: Which Jewish duties encourage helping victims?
flashcards.a: Pikuach nefesh (saving life), tikkun olam (repairing the world) and tzedakah (charity).

flashcards.q: Which verse says helping the needy is like helping Jesus?
flashcards.a: 'Whatever you did for one of the least of these... you did for me' (Matthew 25:40).

flashcards.q: Why might a non-religious person help war victims?
flashcards.a: Compassion and human rights, for example through the Red Cross.

flashcards.q: What is a refugee?
flashcards.a: A person forced to leave their country because of war or persecution.

flashcards.q: Who said 'If you want peace, work for justice', and when?
flashcards.a: Pope Paul VI, in his World Day of Peace message of 1972. It means peace cannot last without fairness.

flashcards.q: What does Mishnah Yoma 8:9 teach about Yom Kippur and forgiveness?
flashcards.a: Yom Kippur atones for sins against God, but not for wrongs against another person until you have made peace with that person.

flashcards.q: Complete: 'Justice, justice you shall ...' (Deuteronomy 16:20)
flashcards.a: '... pursue.' Jews must actively work for justice.

flashcards.q: What is the Community of the Cross of Nails?
flashcards.a: A worldwide reconciliation network that grew from Coventry Cathedral, bombed in 1940, where the words 'Father forgive' were written on the ruins.

flashcards.q: What was South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission?
flashcards.a: A body chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu after apartheid, where victims told their stories and offenders who told the whole truth could apply for amnesty.

flashcards.q: Which verse says God gave Christians 'the ministry of reconciliation'?
flashcards.a: 2 Corinthians 5:18.

flashcards.q: On which three things does the world stand, according to Pirkei Avot 1:18?
flashcards.a: Justice, truth and peace.

flashcards.q: What is The Forgiveness Project?
flashcards.a: A secular UK charity founded in 2004 that shares true stories of victims and offenders to show how forgiveness and reconciliation can happen.

flashcards.q: Which Jesus quote shows forgiveness even of his killers?
flashcards.a: 'Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34).

flashcards.q: What does Sanhedrin 72a teach about self-defence?
flashcards.a: 'If someone comes to kill you, rise and kill him first.' Judaism allows force to save your own life.

flashcards.q: What happened at Heaton Park synagogue on 2 October 2025?
flashcards.a: A terrorist attack on Yom Kippur at the synagogue in Manchester; two people were killed. It is a recent example of terrorism targeting a religious community.

flashcards.q: What was the UK terrorism threat level in November 2026?
flashcards.a: Severe (an attack is highly likely). It was raised from substantial on 30 April 2026.

flashcards.q: Which UK law protects the right to peaceful protest?
flashcards.a: The Human Rights Act 1998 (Articles 10 and 11: freedom of expression and of assembly). The Public Order Act 2023 added new protest offences.

flashcards.q: Give two Bible passages some Christians use to argue force can be right.
flashcards.a: Jesus overturning the tables in the Temple (John 2:15) and 'let him sell his cloak, and buy a sword' (Luke 22:36).

flashcards.q: How would a utilitarian judge violent protest?
flashcards.a: By its consequences: does it bring the greatest good for the greatest number? Usually it causes more harm than good.

flashcards.q: Which Bible verse links wars to selfish desire?
flashcards.a: James 4:1-2: wars and fights come from the desires that battle within you.

flashcards.q: Why did Britain go to war in 1939?
flashcards.a: Because Germany invaded Poland, which Britain had promised to defend. Not because of the Holocaust.

flashcards.q: What did a Jewish king need before fighting an optional war?
flashcards.a: Approval from the Great Sanhedrin of 71 judges (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:5).

flashcards.q: Give a modern example of a war of self-defence.
flashcards.a: Ukraine defending itself since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

flashcards.q: How did the rabbis understand 'an eye for an eye'?
flashcards.a: As fair compensation decided by a court, not as permission for personal revenge.

flashcards.q: Name the three kinds of weapons of mass destruction.
flashcards.a: Nuclear, chemical and biological weapons.

flashcards.q: What is the TPNW and has the UK joined?
flashcards.a: The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, in force since January 2021, bans nuclear weapons. The UK and the other nuclear-armed states have not joined (as of 2026).

flashcards.q: What did Pope Leo XIV say about nuclear weapons in May 2026?
flashcards.a: That the Church has spoken out against all nuclear weapons, so there is no doubt on that point.

flashcards.q: What did the Church of England General Synod decide in 1983 and 2018?
flashcards.a: 1983: rejected unilateral disarmament but said first use could never be justified. 2018: urged the government to respond positively to the nuclear ban treaty.

flashcards.q: What happened to the New START treaty in 2026?
flashcards.a: It expired on 5 February 2026, leaving no treaty limiting US and Russian nuclear weapons.

flashcards.q: How is Shevuot 35b used in Jewish arguments about WMD?
flashcards.a: It is often explained as forbidding a war that would kill more than one sixth of a population, which WMD would do.

flashcards.q: What is unilateral disarmament?
flashcards.a: One country giving up its weapons without waiting for others to do the same.

flashcards.q: What three conditions did Aquinas set out for a just war?
flashcards.a: Proper (legitimate) authority, a just cause and right intention.

flashcards.q: What does Catholic Catechism paragraph 2309 contain?
flashcards.a: Strict conditions for legitimate defence by military force, based on just war thinking.

flashcards.q: Which church leaders questioned the 2003 invasion of Iraq?
flashcards.a: Pope John Paul II and Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams, partly because it lacked clear UN approval and was not a last resort.

flashcards.q: Give two Torah limits on how war is fought.
flashcards.a: Offer peace first (Deuteronomy 20:10) and do not cut down fruit trees (Deuteronomy 20:19).

flashcards.q: What did Augustine say was the aim of war?
flashcards.a: 'We go to war that we may have peace': the only right intention is to restore peace.

flashcards.q: Who were the Maccabees, and how are they remembered?
flashcards.a: Jewish rebels who fought the Greek ruler Antiochus IV in the 2nd century BCE after he banned Judaism. Their rededication of the Temple is remembered at Hanukkah.

flashcards.q: What did the World Russian People's Council say in March 2024?
flashcards.a: It called Russia's war in Ukraine a 'Holy War'. Many church leaders and the World Council of Churches rejected this.

flashcards.q: What was the Day of Pardon in 2000?
flashcards.a: Pope John Paul II asked forgiveness for past sins of Christians, including violence in the service of the faith such as in the Crusades.

flashcards.q: Which pope called the First Crusade, and when?
flashcards.a: Pope Urban II, in 1095.

flashcards.q: Give two reasons why a conflict might be called a holy war.
flashcards.a: It is authorised by a religious leader, and fought for God or to defend the faith or holy places (accept: fighters expect spiritual rewards).

flashcards.q: What did Quakers declare to Charles II in 1660?
flashcards.a: That they 'utterly deny all outward wars and strife, and fightings with outward weapons, for any end'.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between absolute and relative pacifism?
flashcards.a: Absolute: violence is always wrong, even in self-defence. Relative: war is generally wrong but force may be needed in extreme cases.

flashcards.q: Who is Leymah Gbowee?
flashcards.a: A Liberian Christian who led Christian and Muslim women in prayer and protest for peace, helping end Liberia's civil war in 2003. Nobel Peace Prize 2011.

flashcards.q: What did the Community of Sant'Egidio achieve in 1992?
flashcards.a: It helped negotiate the peace agreement that ended Mozambique's civil war.

flashcards.q: What kind of peace did Pope Leo XIV call for when elected in 2025?
flashcards.a: A peace that is 'unarmed and disarming'.

flashcards.q: Name a Jewish organisation that works for peace and human rights.
flashcards.a: Rabbis for Human Rights (Israel, founded 1988) or the Jewish Peace Fellowship (USA, 1941). The Council of Christians and Jews (UK, 1942) builds interfaith understanding.

flashcards.q: Is mainstream Judaism pacifist?
flashcards.a: No. Peace is highly valued, but self-defence and defensive war are allowed and can be a duty to save life.

flashcards.q: Who was Dietrich Bonhoeffer?
flashcards.a: A German Lutheran pastor, once a pacifist, who joined resistance to Hitler and was executed in 1945. Used as an argument against absolute pacifism.

flashcards.q: What is World Jewish Relief and what does it do in Ukraine?
flashcards.a: A British Jewish charity founded in 1933 to help Jews escape Nazi Germany. Since 2022 it has provided food, medicine, heating, shelter and home repairs for vulnerable people in Ukraine.

flashcards.q: What is CAFOD?
flashcards.a: The Catholic aid agency for England and Wales (founded 1962), part of Caritas Internationalis.

flashcards.q: Which Torah verse tells Jews to love the stranger?
flashcards.a: Leviticus 19:34 (also Deuteronomy 10:19): 'for you were strangers in the land of Egypt'.

flashcards.q: What is Christian Aid's slogan?
flashcards.a: 'We believe in life before death.'

flashcards.q: Give three ways individual believers can help victims of war.
flashcards.a: Donate or volunteer, pray, welcome refugees (for example Homes for Ukraine), campaign for civilians to be protected.

quiz.q: Which term means making up and rebuilding a relationship after conflict?
quiz.why: Reconciliation means restoring friendly relations after a conflict.

quiz.q: In Judaism, what is the word for peace and wholeness?
quiz.why: Shalom means peace, wholeness and well-being.

quiz.q: Which Bible quote does a Christian most likely use to show peace is a duty?
quiz.why: Matthew 5:9 links peacemaking directly with being a child of God.

quiz.q: Why do Christians say life is sacred?
options: Because humans live a long time
Because humans are made in God's image
Because humans are the strongest animals
quiz.why: Genesis 1:27 teaches that humans are made in God's image.

quiz.q: Which best defines terrorism?
options: Violence against civilians to cause fear and win political aims
quiz.why: Terrorism uses violence and threats, usually against civilians, for political aims.

quiz.q: What did Jesus say to Peter at his arrest?
quiz.why: Matthew 26:52 shows Jesus rejecting violence.

quiz.q: Which Jewish duty puts saving life first?
quiz.why: Pikuach nefesh means saving a life takes priority over almost everything.

quiz.q: Martin Luther King is an example of which approach?
quiz.why: King led peaceful campaigns against racism.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a reason for war listed by AQA?
quiz.why: AQA lists greed, self-defence and retaliation as reasons for war. Reconciliation is rebuilding relationships after conflict.

quiz.q: Fighting to protect your country from attack is called:
quiz.why: Self-defence is the most widely accepted reason for war.

quiz.q: Which teaching best opposes retaliation?
options: Do not repay evil for evil
quiz.why: Romans 12:17 tells Christians not to repay evil for evil.

quiz.q: War between groups inside one country is:
quiz.why: A civil war is internal armed conflict.

quiz.q: What is nuclear deterrence?
options: Having weapons to put off attackers
quiz.why: Deterrence relies on the threat of retaliation to stop attack.

quiz.q: In which year were nuclear weapons used in war?
quiz.why: Hiroshima and Nagasaki were bombed in August 1945.

quiz.q: A key just war problem with nuclear weapons is that they:
options: Are too weak to win a war
Cannot protect civilians or be proportionate
quiz.why: They cause indiscriminate harm to civilians, which breaks just war rules.

quiz.q: Which Christian group is firmly opposed to nuclear weapons?
quiz.why: Quakers are opposed because of their Peace Testimony.

quiz.q: Who developed the just war criteria in the 13th century?
quiz.why: Aquinas built on Augustine and set out the criteria.

quiz.q: Which criterion means all peaceful options have been tried?
quiz.why: Last resort means war only after other methods fail.

quiz.q: A war that targets civilians breaks which criterion?
quiz.why: Discrimination protects civilians.

quiz.q: What is milchemet mitzvah?
quiz.why: It is a war Jews are required to fight, such as self-defence.

quiz.q: A war fought for a religious cause and approved by God is a:
quiz.why: This is the definition of holy war.

quiz.q: The Crusades were mainly fought to:
quiz.why: They aimed to take control of the Holy Land, called by the Pope.

quiz.q: Which conflict is often used as an example of religion linked to violence?
quiz.why: The Troubles in Northern Ireland involved religious and political identities.

quiz.q: Why do many Christians reject holy war?
options: It goes against Jesus' call to love enemies
It is banned by the United Nations
quiz.why: Matthew 5:44 calls Christians to love enemies.

quiz.q: The Quakers' commitment to peace is called the:
quiz.why: The Peace Testimony is the Quaker commitment to peace.

quiz.q: Which Christian founded the Corrymeela community in 1965?
quiz.why: Ray Davey and others founded Corrymeela in Northern Ireland.

quiz.q: Desmond Doss, a pacifist, served in the Second World War as:
quiz.why: Doss refused weapons but treated the wounded.

quiz.q: Which is an argument against pacifism?
quiz.why: Critics say force may be needed to protect the innocent.

quiz.q: Christian Aid was founded in 1945 to help:
quiz.why: It began in 1945 as help for refugees in Europe after the Second World War.

quiz.q: Which parable inspires care for victims of war?
quiz.why: The Good Samaritan shows love for a stranger in need.

quiz.q: The Jewish duty of charity is:
quiz.why: Tzedakah means charity and justice.

quiz.q: Caritas is:
quiz.why: Caritas is a worldwide network of Catholic charities.

quiz.q: Which word means pardoning someone for a wrong and letting go of the wish for revenge?
quiz.why: Forgiveness is showing grace and mercy and pardoning a wrongdoer.

quiz.q: Which source is best for the Jewish duty to work for justice?
quiz.why: 'Justice, justice you shall pursue' (Deuteronomy 16:20) is a Torah command to work for justice.

quiz.q: According to Mishnah Yoma 8:9, what must a Jew do before Yom Kippur can atone for harming a friend?
options: Make peace with the friend first
quiz.why: Wrongs between people need the person wronged to be appeased; Yom Kippur atones only for sins against God.

quiz.q: A Christian group brings former enemies together to rebuild trust after a war. Which idea are they working for?
quiz.why: Reconciliation means restoring friendly relationships after conflict.

quiz.q: Which source would a Jew most likely use to show violence is allowed in self-defence?
quiz.why: Sanhedrin 72a: 'If someone comes to kill you, rise and kill him first.' The others are Christian teachings against violence.

quiz.q: Which is the odd one out?
quiz.why: A riot is violent protest; the others are peaceful forms of protest.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the Jewish view of violence?
options: Violence is never allowed, even to save life
Violence is a duty to spread the faith
Violence is wrong except where needed to defend life
quiz.why: Judaism is not pacifist: force is allowed to defend life, but revenge is forbidden (Leviticus 19:18).

quiz.q: Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, partly to gain control of its oil. Which reason for war does this best show?
quiz.why: Fighting to gain resources such as oil is greed.

quiz.q: A country is bombed and, a month later, bombs the attacker's cities to punish it. This is best described as:
quiz.why: Hitting back to punish harm already done is retaliation, not defence against an ongoing attack.

quiz.q: Which source would a Jew use to reject revenge as a reason for war?
quiz.why: Leviticus 19:18 says 'You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge'.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the Church of England's position on nuclear weapons?
options: It demands the UK scraps Trident at once
It accepts deterrence as a lesser evil but says first use could never be justified
It supports using them first if needed
quiz.why: Synod rejected unilateral disarmament in 1983 but condemned first use, and in 2018 urged positive engagement with the ban treaty.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a weapon of mass destruction?
quiz.why: A rifle targets individuals; the others are chemical, nuclear and biological WMD.

quiz.q: A student writes only about whether it is right to drop a nuclear bomb. The question asked about countries having a nuclear deterrent. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, use and possession are the same
They should have written about chemical weapons
They answered about use, not possession
quiz.why: Examiners gave no marks to answers about use when the question asked about having a deterrent.

quiz.q: A country bombs a city centre, killing thousands of civilians, to frighten the enemy. Which just war criterion is most clearly broken?
quiz.why: Discrimination forbids deliberately targeting civilians.

quiz.q: Which is a weakness of the just war theory?
options: Both sides often claim their cause is just
quiz.why: People disagree about whether the criteria are met, and each side usually believes it is in the right.

quiz.q: Which Jewish festival remembers a victory in a war for religious freedom?
quiz.why: Hanukkah remembers the Maccabees' victory and the rededication of the Temple.

quiz.q: Which is the best evidence that the Troubles were not only about religion?
options: The main dispute was whether Northern Ireland belonged to the UK or Ireland
quiz.why: Religious identity overlapped with a political dispute about which state Northern Ireland should belong to.

quiz.q: In 2024, which religious body described the war in Ukraine as a 'Holy War'?
quiz.why: The council, headed by Patriarch Kirill, issued the decree; the World Council of Churches criticised it.

quiz.q: Which group's view is the clearest contrast with Quaker pacifism?
options: Mainstream Judaism, which allows defensive war
quiz.why: Mennonites, the Fellowship of Reconciliation and the Peace Pledge Union are all pacifist; mainstream Judaism allows defensive war.

quiz.q: Which person was a Liberian peace activist awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2011?
quiz.why: Leymah Gbowee mobilised Christian and Muslim women for peace in Liberia.

quiz.q: Which of these is a WAY (not a reason) a believer could be a peacemaker?
options: Because Jesus said 'Blessed are the peacemakers'
Because humans are made in God's image
Mediating between two groups in conflict
Because of the sanctity of life
quiz.why: Examiners want actions for 'ways' questions; the others are reasons.

quiz.q: Which Jewish charity began in 1933 helping Jews escape Nazi Germany and now helps people in Ukraine?
quiz.why: World Jewish Relief began as the Central British Fund in 1933.

quiz.q: A question asks for 'two ways' victims of war are helped by religious organisations. Which answer is best?
options: Providing emergency shelter and medical care
quiz.why: 'Ways' needs actions. Naming organisations or giving reasons does not answer the question.

quiz.q: Which source best supports helping victims on the enemy's side?
quiz.why: 'If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat' (Proverbs 25:21).

truefalse.s: In Judaism, shalom means only the absence of war.
truefalse.why: Shalom also means wholeness, harmony and well-being, not just no fighting.

truefalse.s: Many Christians believe a person can be forgiven and still be punished.
truefalse.why: Forgiveness is about letting go of hatred and revenge; justice can still be done.

truefalse.s: Jewish teaching says Yom Kippur automatically removes every wrong done to other people.
truefalse.why: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 says wrongs against people are not atoned until the person wronged has been appeased.

truefalse.s: Pope Paul VI linked peace to justice, saying 'If you want peace, work for justice'.
truefalse.why: This was the title of his 1972 World Day of Peace message.

truefalse.s: Reconciliation means punishing the side that started a conflict.
truefalse.why: Reconciliation means restoring friendly relationships, not punishment.

truefalse.s: Humanists can value forgiveness without believing in God.
truefalse.why: Many humanists see forgiveness as good for the victim's well-being and for society; The Forgiveness Project is a secular charity.

truefalse.s: Judaism is a pacifist religion that forbids all violence, even in self-defence.
truefalse.why: The Torah and Talmud allow force in self-defence (Exodus 22:2, Sanhedrin 72a).

truefalse.s: In UK law, serious damage to property can count as terrorism if it is done to influence the government or intimidate the public.
truefalse.why: The Terrorism Act 2000 definition includes serious damage to property for a political, religious or ideological cause.

truefalse.s: Martin Luther King used violent protest to win civil rights.
truefalse.why: King, a Baptist minister, used non-violent methods such as marches and boycotts.

truefalse.s: Some Christians use Jesus overturning the tables in the Temple to argue that force against injustice can be right.
truefalse.why: John 2:15 is used this way, though others say Jesus did not attack people.

truefalse.s: All Christians agree that violence is always wrong.
truefalse.why: Pacifists say it is always wrong, but most Christians accept force as a last resort in self-defence or to protect others.

truefalse.s: Britain declared war on Germany in 1939 because of the Holocaust.
truefalse.why: Britain went to war because Germany invaded Poland; this was a common mistake noted by examiners.

truefalse.s: In Judaism, a war of self-defence is an obligatory war.
truefalse.why: Defensive war is milchemet mitzvah, which everyone must support.

truefalse.s: Retaliation and self-defence mean the same thing.
truefalse.why: Self-defence stops an attack; retaliation is paying back harm already done.

truefalse.s: Article 51 of the UN Charter recognises a nation's right to self-defence.
truefalse.why: International law allows self-defence but not aggression.

truefalse.s: Pacifist Christians accept self-defence as a good reason for war.
truefalse.why: Pacifists reject all war, even defensive war.

truefalse.s: The UK has signed the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.
truefalse.why: As of 2026, none of the nine nuclear-armed states, including the UK, has joined the TPNW.

truefalse.s: Catholic teaching under recent popes says even possessing nuclear weapons is immoral.
truefalse.why: Pope Francis condemned possession in 2017 and 2019, and Pope Leo XIV reaffirmed opposition to all nuclear weapons in 2026.

truefalse.s: Weapons of mass destruction means only nuclear weapons.
truefalse.why: WMD also include chemical and biological weapons.

truefalse.s: Some religious believers accept having nuclear weapons as a deterrent while saying they must never be used.
truefalse.why: Examiners credited this view; for example the Church of England has accepted deterrence as a lesser evil.

truefalse.s: Nuclear weapons have been used in war many times since 1945.
truefalse.why: They have only been used in war twice, on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.

truefalse.s: The just war criteria are listed word for word in the Bible.
truefalse.why: They were developed by Christian thinkers such as Augustine and Aquinas, using biblical ideas.

truefalse.s: Proportionality means the harm caused by a war must not outweigh the good it achieves.
truefalse.why: It also means using no more force than necessary.

truefalse.s: Holy war and just war are two names for the same idea.
truefalse.why: Just war is about fair reasons and limits; holy war is fought for a religious cause, believed to be supported by God.

truefalse.s: In Jewish law an optional war needed the approval of the Sanhedrin.
truefalse.why: Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:5 says a king could only lead an optional war with the court of 71.

truefalse.s: A war is a holy war simply because the soldiers fighting it are religious.
truefalse.why: Religion must be the reason for the war, for example authorised by a religious leader to defend or spread the faith.

truefalse.s: Most Christians today believe the Crusades went against Jesus' teaching.
truefalse.why: Many church leaders, including Pope John Paul II in 2000, have asked forgiveness for violence done in the name of the faith.

truefalse.s: Political ideologies such as fascism have also caused major wars.
truefalse.why: Non-religious beliefs, such as Nazism, drove the Second World War, so belief in general, not only religion, can cause conflict.

truefalse.s: Most Jews today believe that holy wars should still be declared.
truefalse.why: Most Jews say there is no authority today to declare such a war; only defensive war is accepted.

truefalse.s: All Christians are pacifists.
truefalse.why: Most Christians accept just war theory; Quakers and Mennonites are the main pacifist groups.

truefalse.s: Mainstream Judaism is not a pacifist tradition.
truefalse.why: Judaism allows defensive war and self-defence, though it values peace highly.

truefalse.s: Pacifists simply do nothing when there is conflict.
truefalse.why: Many pacifists work actively for peace, for example through aid, protest, mediation or serving as medics.

truefalse.s: Corrymeela was founded in 1965 and marked 60 years of peacebuilding in 2025.
truefalse.why: Ray Davey founded it in 1965 in Ballycastle, Northern Ireland.

truefalse.s: Some non-religious people are pacifists.
truefalse.why: For example, the atheist philosopher Bertrand Russell was imprisoned in 1918 for campaigning against war.

truefalse.s: Christian Aid only helps Christians.
truefalse.why: Christian Aid helps people in need regardless of religion, following the Good Samaritan.

truefalse.s: Tzedakah is seen in Judaism as a duty of justice, not just an optional act of kindness.
truefalse.why: The word is linked to tzedek, justice.

truefalse.s: The Red Cross is a Christian religious charity.
truefalse.why: Despite its symbol, the Red Cross is a neutral humanitarian organisation, not a religious one.

truefalse.s: The parable of the Sheep and Goats teaches that helping people in need is like helping Jesus.
truefalse.why: Matthew 25:40: 'you did it to me'.

short.q: Give one meaning of the word justice.
short.a: Bringing about what is right and fair (accept: making up for a wrong; fairness under the law).

short.q: Give the Hebrew word for peace.
short.a: Shalom.

short.q: Name one example of reconciliation after conflict.
short.a: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (accept: Coventry Cathedral's Community of the Cross of Nails; Corrymeela; the Good Friday Agreement).

short.q: Give one teaching of Jesus about forgiveness.
short.a: Forgive seventy times seven (accept: the Lord's Prayer, forgive us as we forgive others; 'Father, forgive them').

short.q: Give one example of non-violent protest.
short.a: A march (accept: petition, vigil, boycott, sit-in, strike).

short.q: Give one reason why religious believers condemn terrorism.
short.a: It deliberately kills innocent people (accept: breaks 'You shall not murder'; goes against the sanctity of life; love your neighbour).

short.q: Name one terrorist attack in the UK.
short.a: The 7 July 2005 London bombings (accept: Manchester Arena 2017; Heaton Park synagogue, Manchester, 2025).

short.q: Give one situation in which most Christians would accept the use of violence.
short.a: Self-defence (accept: protecting innocent people; as a last resort in a just war).

short.q: Give one reason for war named in the AQA specification.
short.a: Greed (accept: self-defence; retaliation).

short.q: Give one example of greed as a cause of war.
short.a: Fighting to take land or oil (accept: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990).

short.q: Give the meaning of retaliation.
short.a: Deliberately harming someone in return for harm they have done (accept: hitting back, revenge).

short.q: Name the UK's nuclear weapons system.
short.a: Trident.

short.a: Just cause (accept: legitimate authority, right intention, last resort, reasonable chance of success, proportionality, discrimination).

Christian: do not meet just war rules of proportionality and discrimination
Jewish: pikuach nefesh, protecting life, so WMD are wrong

exam.q: 'Nuclear weapons can never be justified.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Many Christians agree with this statement. Nuclear weapons kill huge numbers of innocent people, so they appear to break the commandment 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13). Christians believe life is sacred because humans are made in God's image, so a weapon that can destroy whole cities treats life as worthless. Nuclear weapons also fail the just war rules of proportionality and discrimination because they cannot avoid harming civilians. Pope Francis said in 2017 that even possessing them should be condemned, and Quakers campaign for disarmament. This is a strong argument because Hiroshima shows the scale of suffering and the damage lasts for generations.

However, others disagree. Some Christians and Jews argue that nuclear deterrence has helped keep the peace since 1945, because no country wants to risk being destroyed. Judaism teaches that saving life (pikuach nefesh) is vital, and some Jews argue that after the Holocaust a country must be able to defend its people. Some Christians accept possession as the lesser evil while hoping for disarmament, since the Bible accepts that there is 'a time for war and a time for peace' (Ecclesiastes 3:8). This argument is weaker, because deterrence only works if a country is willing to use the weapons, which most religious leaders say is wrong, and accidents or terrorists could still cause a disaster. A non-religious person might add that the billions spent on Trident could fund health and education.

Overall, I think the statement is mostly convincing. The sanctity of life and just war rules make actual use almost impossible to justify. But the word 'never' is strong, because possession as a deterrent can be seen as a lesser evil even if it is not ideal. So believers have strong reasons to say use cannot be justified, but they disagree about whether keeping the weapons is acceptable.
for: Nuclear weapons kill innocents and break 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13); sanctity of life, made in God's image
Fail just war rules of proportionality and discrimination; Pope Francis 2017; Quakers and Pax Christi back disarmament; cost and risk of accidents
against: Deterrence has helped keep peace since 1945; some Christians accept possession as a lesser evil
Jewish pikuach nefesh and Holocaust memory: defending the people; a time for war (Ecclesiastes 3:8); countries need protection
exam.conclusion: The sanctity of life and just war rules make use very hard to justify, but possession as deterrence can be seen as a lesser evil, so 'never' is too strong a word for possession.
points: Developed arguments on both sides with religious teachings
Evaluation of strength of each argument
Justified conclusion
Non-religious views may be credited if relevant

exam.q: 'It is impossible to fight a just war today.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some people agree that a just war is impossible today. Just war theory, developed by Augustine and Aquinas, says that war must be a last resort, proportionate, and must protect civilians. Modern weapons such as missiles and bombs make this very hard, because they often kill civilians. Christian pacifists such as Quakers argue that war never meets these rules, quoting Jesus' command to 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44). This is a strong argument because many modern wars have caused huge civilian suffering and refugee crises.

On the other hand, many Christians believe a just war is still possible. The theory is a guide to judge each case, not a promise that war is good. For example, a defensive war to stop a brutal invader could have a just cause and right intention. Psalm 82:4 tells believers to 'rescue the weak and the needy', which supports using force to protect others. Jews also teach that defensive war can be an obligation, because saving life (pikuach nefesh) matters most. International law also allows self-defence, so non-religious people may agree that some wars can be justified. This argument is persuasive because it accepts that doing nothing against great evil may also be wrong, though it depends on leaders honestly following the rules.

In my view, a just war is difficult but not impossible. Modern conflict often fails the tests of proportionality and discrimination, but a limited defensive war could still meet all the criteria. The theory remains useful because it forces leaders to justify their actions. So the statement is too strong, although it is right that few modern wars meet every condition.
for: Modern weapons make proportionality and discrimination hard; civilians suffer
Pacifist Christians: Jesus' teaching, Matthew 5:44; Quakers; Exodus 20:13
against: Just war theory is a guide to judge each war; defence of the innocent (Psalm 82:4)
Jewish teaching: defensive war obligatory; pikuach nefesh; self-defence in international law
exam.conclusion: A just war is difficult but not impossible: a limited defensive war could meet the criteria, so the statement is too strong, though few modern wars satisfy every condition.

exam.q: 'Religion causes more war than peace.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some people agree that religion causes more war than peace. History shows religious wars, such as the Crusades, which were called by the Pope to take control of the Holy Land. Religion also forms part of conflicts today, such as the Troubles in Northern Ireland and the conflict in Israel and Palestine, where religious identity divides people. Some extremists even claim holy war to justify terrorism. Non-religious people, such as many Humanists, argue that when people believe God is on their side, they may find it easier to justify violence. This is a fair argument, but it can be exaggerated because most conflicts also involve land, power and politics.

On the other hand, many believers argue that religion promotes peace more than it causes war. Jesus taught 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9) and 'Love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44), and Jewish teaching values shalom and says that saving life is a duty. Religious groups have worked hard for peace, such as Corrymeela, which brings people from different sides in Northern Ireland together, and Pax Christi, and Martin Luther King and Desmond Tutu were driven by Christian beliefs. Most Christians today reject holy war. This argument is strong because it describes what the main teachings actually say and what religious people do every day, not just what extremists claim.

Overall, I think the statement is not convincing. Religion has been linked to violence at times, but usually alongside politics and identity, whereas teachings and actions for peace are central and widespread. It is more accurate to say religion can be used to support either war or peace, depending on how people interpret it.
for: Crusades, Troubles, Israel-Palestine; religious extremism; claims of holy war
Non-religious view that belief in God can justify violence; religion divides identities
against: Jesus' teaching on peace (Matthew 5:9, 5:44); Jewish shalom and pikuach nefesh
Peacemaking: Corrymeela, Pax Christi, King, Tutu; most believers reject holy war; many wars are political
exam.conclusion: Religion has been linked to violence, but teachings and actions for peace are widespread, and many conflicts involve politics and identity, so the statement is not convincing.
points: Both sides with developed religious teachings
Evaluation: weigh religion against political causes
Conclusion that follows the argument
Non-religious views allowed

exam.q: 'Christians should always be pacifists.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some Christians strongly agree. Jesus taught 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9) and told his followers to 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44). When he was arrested he told Peter to put his sword away. The commandment 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13) is also used to argue that all killing is wrong. Quakers, for instance, follow a Peace Testimony and believe there is something of God in everyone, so they could never kill. This is a powerful argument because it follows Jesus' own example, and the early Church often refused to fight.

Other Christians disagree. They argue that sometimes force is needed to stop great evil, so pacifism could leave innocent people unprotected. Just war theory, set out by Augustine and Aquinas, says war can be justified if it is a last resort, has a just cause and is proportionate. Psalm 82:4 tells believers to 'rescue the weak and the needy', and Dietrich Bonhoeffer joined resistance to Hitler because he believed doing nothing would be worse. The Bible also says there is 'a time for war and a time for peace' (Ecclesiastes 3:8). This argument is also strong because it tackles the problem of protecting others, but it depends on leaders following the criteria honestly, which is difficult.

In my view, the statement is not convincing as a rule for all Christians. Pacifism is a powerful moral witness and fits Jesus' teaching, but Christians disagree about how to apply love in a world where aggression exists. A better conclusion is that all Christians should work for peace and avoid violence wherever possible, while accepting that some, with a clear conscience, may support limited force as a last resort.
for: Jesus' teaching on peace and enemies; refusing to fight at arrest; Exodus 20:13
Quakers and Peace Testimony; early Church example; non-violent protest of King
against: Force may be needed to protect innocents; just war theory; Psalm 82:4
Bonhoeffer; Ecclesiastes 3:8; evil must sometimes be resisted
exam.conclusion: Pacifism is a powerful witness and fits Jesus' teaching, but Christians disagree on how to apply love, so 'always' is too strong. All Christians should work for peace, but some accept force as a last resort.
points: Both sides with religious teachings
Evaluate each argument
Justified conclusion
Non-religious views may be credited

exam.q: 'Violent protest is sometimes the only way to bring change.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some people agree with the statement. When people are denied rights and peaceful protest is ignored, some argue violence may be the only way to be heard. Malcolm X argued that Black Americans might need to defend themselves, and some of the Suffragettes damaged property because votes for women were ignored. A few Christians say violence can be the lesser evil against a cruel regime, and Jews accept force to defend life (Exodus 22:2). Non-religious people may add that some governments only respond to pressure. This argument has some strength because history shows peaceful protest sometimes fails at first, but it is weakened because violence often leads to deaths and riots and can lose public support.

Others disagree strongly. Christians believe in love and forgiveness. Jesus said 'Put your sword back in its place, for all who draw the sword will die by the sword' (Matthew 26:52) and 'Love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44). Martin Luther King, a Baptist minister, achieved major change in civil rights in the USA by using marches and boycotts. Jews also believe in the sanctity of life, and violence puts innocent people at risk. This argument is very strong because peaceful protest has produced lasting change, and violence often damages the cause it supports.

Overall, I find the statement unconvincing. Violence might sometimes force attention, but religious teachings and examples such as King show peaceful methods can also work and avoid harming innocents. 'Only way' is too strong, because other options usually exist, so most believers would say violent protest should not be the answer.
for: Peaceful protest ignored; Malcolm X; Suffragettes; lesser evil against injustice
Jewish self-defence (Exodus 22:2); non-religious view that pressure can force change
against: Jesus: Matthew 26:52, 5:44; love and forgiveness; Romans 12:21
Martin Luther King's success; sanctity of life; violence risks harm and loses support
exam.conclusion: Violence may gain attention but peaceful protest can succeed and avoids harming innocents, so 'the only way' is too strong.
points: Both sides with religious teachings
Evaluate strengths and weaknesses
Conclusion
Non-religious views allowed

exam.q: Explain two similar religious beliefs about the importance of peace. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.
points: Christian: Jesus the Prince of Peace taught 'Blessed are the peacemakers', so peace is a duty for his followers
Christian: humans are made in God's image, so peace protects sacred life
Jewish: shalom is God's gift and a greeting; Hillel taught to love peace and pursue it
Jewish: the prophets look forward to a messianic age of peace (Isaiah 2:4, Micah 4:3)
Credit similar points across or within traditions, each developed
exam.model:
One similar belief is that peace is something God wants for the world. Christians call Jesus the 'Prince of Peace', and Jews share the prophets' hope for a time when nations will no longer go to war (Isaiah 2:4), so both work and pray for that future.
A second similar belief is that peace has to be actively pursued, not just waited for. Jesus said peacemakers are children of God, and Jews follow Hillel's teaching to be 'loving peace and pursuing peace', so believers in both faiths try to settle quarrels and build harmony in their own communities.

exam.q: Explain two religious beliefs about reconciliation. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
points: Belief 1: Christians believe God reconciled people to himself through Jesus, so they must reconcile with others
Source: 2 Corinthians 5:18, 'the ministry of reconciliation'
Application: Coventry Cathedral's Community of the Cross of Nails, Corrymeela
Belief 2: reconciliation with others comes before worship
Source: Matthew 5:23-24, or Mishnah Yoma 8:9 (Jewish: appease the person you wronged before Yom Kippur)

exam.model:
One belief is that Christians have a duty to reconcile people because God first reconciled humans to himself through Jesus' death. St Paul wrote that God 'gave to us the ministry of reconciliation' (2 Corinthians 5:18). This means Christians should help former enemies rebuild trust, as Coventry Cathedral has done since it was bombed in 1940 through its Community of the Cross of Nails.
Another belief, found in Judaism, is that you cannot be right with God while a relationship with another person is broken. The Mishnah (Yoma 8:9) teaches that Yom Kippur only atones for wrongs against another person once you have made peace with them. This means Jews go to people they have hurt before Yom Kippur to apologise and put things right, so reconciliation is built into the religious year.

exam.q: 'After a war, justice is more important than forgiveness.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
for: Victims deserve justice; war crimes must be punished or they may happen again (deterrence); Amos 5:24, Deuteronomy 16:20 'Justice, justice you shall pursue'
Jewish teaching that only the victim can forgive; forgiveness without repentance can feel like injustice; Paul VI: 'If you want peace, work for justice'
Non-religious: international courts and human rights law protect future victims
against: Jesus taught limitless forgiveness (Matthew 18:22) and forgave his killers (Luke 23:34); the Lord's Prayer
Forgiveness breaks cycles of revenge; reconciliation examples: Coventry 'Father forgive', Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission
Humanist view that letting go of hatred helps victims and society heal
exam.conclusion: Justice and forgiveness need each other: forgiveness without justice can feel like approving the wrong, and justice without forgiveness can keep hatred alive. Many believers would say forgiveness is the ultimate goal, but justice must be part of the process.
exam.model:
Some people agree that justice matters most after a war. Victims and their families deserve to see wrongdoers held to account, and if war crimes go unpunished, other leaders may think they can get away with the same. The Bible demands justice: 'Let justice roll on like rivers' (Amos 5:24), and the Torah commands 'Justice, justice you shall pursue' (Deuteronomy 16:20). Many Jews also teach that forgiveness belongs to the victim, so no one can forgive mass murder on behalf of the dead. Non-religious people may support international courts for the same reason: justice protects future victims. This is a strong argument because peace built on ignoring crimes is often fragile, as Pope Paul VI suggested when he said, 'If you want peace, work for justice.'

Others argue that forgiveness is more important. Jesus told Peter to forgive 'seventy times seven' times (Matthew 18:22) and prayed for those crucifying him, 'Father, forgive them' (Luke 23:34). Christians say only forgiveness can end cycles of revenge, which often cause the next war. After Coventry Cathedral was bombed in 1940, its leaders wrote 'Father forgive' on the ruins and built friendships with German cities. In South Africa, Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission put truth and reconciliation before punishment, which helped avoid a civil war. Humanists may add that letting go of hatred helps victims heal. This is also persuasive, though forgiveness can be hard to ask of people who have lost everything, and Tutu's approach left some victims feeling cheated of justice.

In conclusion, I do not think one is simply more important. Forgiveness without any justice can look like approving the wrong, but justice without forgiveness keeps hatred alive. Most religious teaching suggests justice should be done, while forgiveness is the final aim that makes real reconciliation possible.

exam.q: Explain two different beliefs in contemporary British society about the use of violence. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
points: Christian pacifists (Quakers): violence is never right; Matthew 26:52, Matthew 5:39
Most Christians: violence is a last resort for self-defence or protecting others; just war, Catholic Catechism on legitimate defence
Judaism: not pacifist; self-defence allowed (Exodus 22:2, Sanhedrin 72a), but revenge forbidden (Leviticus 19:18)
Must refer to Christianity and at least one other religion; two clearly different beliefs, each developed
exam.model:
One belief, held by Christian pacifists such as Quakers, is that violence is always wrong. They follow Jesus, who told Peter to put away his sword because 'all those who take the sword will die by the sword', so they respond to conflict with non-violent action instead.
A different belief is found in Judaism, which teaches that violence is wrong in general but can be a duty to save life. The Talmud says that if someone comes to kill you, you should rise and kill him first, so Jews may use force to defend themselves or others, though never for revenge.

exam.q: Explain two religious beliefs about violent protest. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
points: Belief 1: violent protest is wrong because Jesus rejected violence and taught love of enemies
Source: Matthew 26:52 or Romans 12:21
Application: support peaceful protest, like Martin Luther King
Belief 2: some say force against injustice can be justified when peaceful methods fail
Source: John 2:15, Jesus overturning the tables; or Exodus 22:2 / Sanhedrin 72a for defending life
Application: damage to property rather than people; a last resort
exam.model:
One belief is that Christians should not use violent protest because Jesus rejected violence. When Peter attacked a servant at Jesus' arrest, Jesus said, 'Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword' (Matthew 26:52). This means Christians should protest in peaceful ways, as the Baptist minister Martin Luther King did with marches and boycotts.
A different belief is that force against serious injustice can sometimes be justified. In John's Gospel, Jesus made a whip and overturned the money changers' tables in the Temple (John 2:15) because they were exploiting worshippers. Some Christians argue this shows that anger and direct action against injustice can be right, though they would still say people must never be harmed, so any action should be a last resort.

exam.q: 'Religious believers should never use violence.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
for: Jesus: Matthew 26:52, 5:39, 5:44; Quaker Peace Testimony; early Christians
Sanctity of life: Exodus 20:13; violence breeds more violence; Romans 12:21
Non-violent success: Martin Luther King; humanist commitment to reason and democracy
against: Self-defence: Exodus 22:2, Sanhedrin 72a; pikuach nefesh may require force
Protecting the innocent: Psalm 82:4; just war; Catholic teaching on legitimate defence; Bonhoeffer
Utilitarian: force may prevent a greater harm
exam.conclusion: Believers should never choose violence for revenge, gain or to force their views, but 'never' is too strong if force is the only way to protect life. Both pacifists and non-pacifists agree violence is a last resort at most.
exam.model:
Many Christians agree with this statement. Jesus told Peter to put away his sword (Matthew 26:52), taught his followers to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:39) and to love their enemies. Quakers follow a Peace Testimony and believe there is 'that of God' in everyone, so harming anyone harms something sacred. The commandment 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13) supports the sanctity of life, and Paul taught believers to 'overcome evil with good' (Romans 12:21). There is also evidence that non-violence works: Martin Luther King won major civil rights changes through marches and boycotts. This is a strong argument because violence usually provokes more violence and hurts innocent people.

However, other believers argue that violence can sometimes be right. Judaism is not pacifist: the Torah allows a householder to defend himself against a burglar at night (Exodus 22:2), and the Talmud says 'If someone comes to kill you, rise and kill him first' (Sanhedrin 72a). Because saving life (pikuach nefesh) is so important, using force to protect people may even be a duty. Most Christians, including the Catholic Church, accept legitimate self-defence, and Psalm 82:4 tells believers to 'rescue the weak and needy'. The German pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer joined the plot against Hitler because he believed doing nothing would allow greater evil. A utilitarian would agree that force can be right if it prevents greater suffering. This is persuasive because refusing to protect a victim can itself seem unloving.

In conclusion, I think the statement is too absolute. Religious teaching is clear that believers should never use violence for revenge, greed or to force their beliefs on others. But where force is the only way to protect innocent life, most Christians and Jews accept it as a last resort, so 'never' goes further than most religious traditions do.

exam.q: 'Retaliation is never a good reason to go to war.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
for: Jesus replaced 'eye for an eye' with turning the other cheek (Matthew 5:38-39); Romans 12:17-19 leave vengeance to God
Leviticus 19:18 forbids vengeance; just war 'right intention' rules out revenge
Utilitarian and humanist: revenge starts cycles of violence and kills innocents
against: Striking back can stop further attacks and protect people (Psalm 82:4); deterrence
Judaism allows force against those who will attack again (Sanhedrin 72a); Exodus 21:24 shows wrongs must be answered
Non-religious: weakness invites aggression; international law allows force to stop continuing attacks
exam.conclusion: Revenge for its own sake is never a good reason in Christian, Jewish or humanist ethics, but a response that stops further attacks is really self-defence, so the statement is right about retaliation in the true sense.
exam.model:
Most religious believers agree with this statement. Jesus replaced the old rule 'an eye for an eye' with the command to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:38-39), and Paul wrote 'Repay no one evil for evil' and told Christians to leave vengeance to God (Romans 12:17-19). Just war theory demands a right intention, and revenge is not one. Judaism agrees: 'You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge' (Leviticus 19:18). Humanists and utilitarians would add that revenge attacks usually start a cycle of violence, so many more innocent people suffer than if the conflict had been stopped. This is a strong argument because history is full of feuds where each side's 'payback' led to the next attack.

On the other hand, some argue that hitting back can be necessary. If a country is attacked and does nothing, the attacker may be encouraged to strike again, so a strong response can protect people in future. Psalm 82:4 tells believers to 'rescue the weak and needy', and the Talmud permits striking first at someone who is coming to kill you (Sanhedrin 72a). Some Jews point to Israel's responses to rocket attacks as defending citizens from further harm. Non-religious realists argue that weakness invites aggression. This argument has some force, but it mostly shows that self-defence and deterrence can be right, not revenge itself. When a response aims to stop continuing attacks, it is really self-defence rather than retaliation.

In conclusion, I agree with the statement. Retaliation in the true sense, harming others simply to pay them back, is rejected by Christian, Jewish and humanist ethics because it is driven by anger, not justice, and usually increases suffering. Where force is needed to prevent further attacks, it should be judged as self-defence under strict rules, not justified as revenge.

exam.q: Explain two different beliefs in contemporary British society about countries having nuclear weapons. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
points: Catholic / Quaker: possession is immoral; Pope Leo XIV 2026, Peace Testimony; campaign for disarmament
Church of England / some Christians: deterrence as lesser evil, keeps peace, but first use never justified
Jewish: some accept deterrence for a nation's survival after the Holocaust; others say mass killing can never be justified (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5)
Must be about having (possession), not just using; Christianity plus another religion
exam.model:
One belief is that it is wrong even to possess nuclear weapons. The Catholic Church teaches this: Pope Leo XIV said in 2026 that the Church opposes all nuclear weapons, because keeping them means being ready to kill millions of innocent people, so Catholics campaign for disarmament.
A different belief, held by some Jews, is that a nation may need nuclear weapons as a deterrent to survive. After the Holocaust, some argue a small country surrounded by enemies must be able to stop attacks, so possessing weapons that are never used can be the lesser evil.

exam.q: 'It is right for countries to keep nuclear weapons as a deterrent.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
for: No war between nuclear powers since 1945; protects citizens and allies; Psalm 82:4 duty to protect
Church of England 1983: deterrence a lesser evil while working for disarmament; some Jews: survival after the Holocaust
Non-religious realist and utilitarian argument: prevents greater harm; UK government policy (Trident, F-35A, 2025)
against: Catholic teaching: possession immoral (Francis 2017, 2019; Leo XIV 2026); Quaker Peace Testimony; Isaiah 2:4
Deterrence requires willingness to murder millions (Exodus 20:13); fails proportionality and discrimination; Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5
Accidents, terrorism, arms race after New START expired 2026; billions could help the poor
exam.conclusion: Deterrence may have helped avoid major war, but it depends on a threat most religious teaching says could never be carried out. Possession as a temporary lesser evil while seriously working for disarmament is the strongest version of the statement.
exam.model:
Some people agree with this statement. Supporters of deterrence point out that no two nuclear powers have fought a full-scale war against each other since 1945, which suggests the fear of retaliation keeps the peace. The UK government believes Trident protects Britain and its NATO allies, and in 2025 announced it would buy jets able to carry nuclear weapons. Some Christians, including the Church of England's General Synod in 1983, have accepted deterrence as a lesser evil in a dangerous world, while saying first use could never be justified. Psalm 82:4 tells believers to protect the weak, and some Jews argue that after the Holocaust a nation must be able to prevent its own destruction. A utilitarian might say deterrence produces the best outcome if it prevents a war that would kill millions.

Others disagree strongly. The Catholic Church now teaches that even possessing nuclear weapons is immoral; Pope Leo XIV said in 2026 that the Church opposes all nuclear weapons. Deterrence only works if leaders are prepared to kill millions of civilians, which would break 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13) and the just war rules of proportionality and discrimination. Jewish teaching that destroying one life is like destroying a whole world (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5) makes mass killing unthinkable. Quakers and CND add that accidents or terrorists could cause disaster, and with New START expiring in 2026 there is a risk of a new arms race. The billions spent could help the poor, as Isaiah 2:4 imagines swords being turned into ploughshares. This argument is strong because a threat to do something deeply evil is hard to call right.

In conclusion, I think deterrence can only be defended as a temporary lesser evil. It may have helped prevent major war, but it rests on a threat that most religious teaching says must never be carried out. So countries may keep nuclear weapons for now only if they are seriously working towards disarmament, which suggests the statement is partly true but not right as a permanent position.

exam.q: Explain two similar religious beliefs about how a war should be fought. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.
points: Christian just war: discrimination, civilians must not be targeted
Christian just war: proportionality, no more force than needed
Jewish: peace offered first (Deuteronomy 20:10); do not destroy trees (Deuteronomy 20:19); leave an escape route
Both traditions: aim of war must be peace, not revenge
exam.model:
One similar belief is that innocent people must be protected in war. Christians who follow just war theory say the rule of discrimination means civilians must never be deliberately attacked, and Jewish tradition similarly teaches that a besieged city should be left open on one side so that those who wish can escape.
A second similar belief is that war must be limited and not cause more destruction than necessary. Christians call this proportionality, and the Torah forbids cutting down fruit trees during a siege (Deuteronomy 20:19), so both traditions say a war that causes needless destruction is wrong.

exam.q: Explain two different beliefs in contemporary British society about pacifism. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
points: Quakers: absolute pacifism; Peace Testimony; that of God in everyone; Matthew 5:9, 5:44
Most Christians (Catholic, Anglican): not pacifist; just war as last resort to protect the innocent
Judaism: not pacifist; defensive war a duty (milchemet mitzvah, pikuach nefesh); yet pursue peace (Pirkei Avot 1:12)
Two clearly different beliefs, Christianity plus another religion
exam.model:
One belief is that pacifism is right. Quakers believe there is 'that of God' in everyone, so killing any person is wrong, and since 1660 their Peace Testimony has led them to refuse to fight and to work for peace instead.
A different belief is held by most Jews, who say pacifism is not required. Judaism teaches that saving life is a duty, so fighting a defensive war (milchemet mitzvah) to protect people can be necessary, even though Jews are also taught to love peace and pursue it.

exam.q: Explain two reasons why religious believers work for reconciliation and peace today. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
points: Reason 1: Jesus called peacemakers children of God
Source: Matthew 5:9
Application: Corrymeela, Sant'Egidio mediation
Reason 2 (Jewish): duty to pursue peace like Aaron
Source: Pirkei Avot 1:12 or Psalm 34:14
Application: interfaith work such as the Council of Christians and Jews; Rabbis for Human Rights
exam.model:
One reason is that Jesus taught that peacemaking is the mark of God's children. In the Sermon on the Mount he said, 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God' (Matthew 5:9). This means Christians see making peace as part of following Jesus, so communities such as Corrymeela in Northern Ireland bring Catholics and Protestants together, and Sant'Egidio helps negotiate peace agreements.
Another reason, from Judaism, is that peace has to be actively chased, not just hoped for. Hillel taught Jews to be 'loving peace and pursuing peace' like Aaron (Pirkei Avot 1:12). This means Jews take practical steps to build peace, for example through interfaith groups such as the Council of Christians and Jews, or Rabbis for Human Rights, which works for justice for both Israelis and Palestinians.

exam.q: Explain two similar religious beliefs about helping victims of war. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.
points: Christian: love your neighbour; Good Samaritan, help strangers and enemies
Christian: Sheep and Goats, serving Jesus by helping the needy
Jewish: pikuach nefesh and tikkun olam, a duty to save life and repair the world
Jewish: love the stranger (Leviticus 19:34); help enemies (Proverbs 25:21)
Similar points, each developed
exam.model:
One similar belief is that victims must be helped whichever side they are on. Christians learn this from the Good Samaritan, who helped a man from a hostile group, and Jews from Proverbs 25:21, 'If your enemy is hungry, give him food', so believers give aid to all victims, not just their own people.
A second similar belief is that helping is a religious duty, not an optional kindness. Christians believe helping the needy is serving Jesus (Matthew 25:40), and Jews see saving life (pikuach nefesh) as a commandment that overrides almost every other, so both give time and money to charities such as Christian Aid or World Jewish Relief.

exam.q: 'Religious believers should do more to help victims of war than to stop wars.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
for: Practical, immediate need: Good Samaritan, Sheep and Goats (Matthew 25:40); pikuach nefesh
Believers have little power over governments but can feed, shelter and heal now: Christian Aid, CAFOD, World Jewish Relief in Ukraine
Humanist: relieve suffering in this life
against: Prevention is better than cure: 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9); 'seek peace and pursue it' (Psalm 34:14)
Peacemaking works: Sant'Egidio in Mozambique, Leymah Gbowee in Liberia, Corrymeela; Pope Leo XIV calls for disarmament
Charities themselves campaign on causes of conflict; justice brings lasting peace (Amos 5:24)
exam.conclusion: Both are religious duties and they are linked. Helping victims is the most immediate, achievable response, but stopping wars prevents future victims, so believers should not choose one over the other.
exam.model:
Some people agree with this statement. When people are injured, starving or homeless, they need help now, and religious teaching is very clear about this. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, the Samaritan did not try to catch the robbers; he bandaged the wounded man and paid for his care. Jesus said that whatever is done for the least of his brothers and sisters is done for him (Matthew 25:40). Judaism teaches that saving a life (pikuach nefesh) overrides almost every other commandment. Ordinary believers have little power over presidents and armies, but through charities such as Christian Aid, CAFOD and World Jewish Relief, which has helped vulnerable people in Ukraine since 2022, they can make a real difference to millions. A humanist would agree that reducing suffering in this life is the priority. This is a strong argument because help for victims is practical and certain to do good.

Others argue that stopping wars should come first, because prevention is better than cure. Jesus said 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9), and the Psalms tell believers to 'seek peace and pursue it' (Psalm 34:14). Religious peacemaking can work: the Catholic community of Sant'Egidio helped end Mozambique's civil war in 1992, and Leymah Gbowee's movement of Christian and Muslim women helped end the war in Liberia. Every war prevented saves thousands of future victims. Many charities also see that aid alone is not enough: Christian Aid campaigns on the causes of conflict, because 'justice' (Amos 5:24) brings lasting peace. This argument is persuasive because helping victims while doing nothing about the causes means the suffering keeps happening.

In conclusion, I disagree that believers should do more of one than the other. Helping victims is the most immediate and achievable duty, and every believer can do it. But peacemaking is also a direct command of Jesus and the prophets, and it prevents victims in the first place. The two belong together, as the many religious organisations that do both show.
